messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Military Medic
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 64

# Case Vignette: Gerald

Gerald is a 67-year-old widowed man who spent the better part of his adult life as a military medic, a career that taught him to stay calm under pressure and to keep moving no matter what was happening around him. He was the man others leaned on in crisis. He knew how to compartmentalize, how to function, how to push through. That identity — steady, capable, unshakeable — is something he held onto long after he retired from service. It is also something that the events of fourteen months ago have quietly, relentlessly dismantled.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn when Gerald's truck was struck by a semi that ran a red light at highway speed. The impact spun his vehicle across two lanes and into a concrete barrier. He was conscious throughout — he remembers the sound of the collision, a noise he describes as nothing like the explosions he heard overseas, somehow worse in its ordinariness. He remembers not being able to move his left arm, the smell of something burning, and the strange, suspended silence that followed before other drivers began to approach. What he cannot stop remembering is looking in the rearview mirror and seeing his own face, and believing with complete certainty that he was about to die.

He did not die. He sustained a fractured clavicle, three broken ribs, and a concussion. He was discharged from the hospital after four days. By every medical measure, he recovered well. But something did not come back with him when he left that hospital.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald found himself unable to sleep for more than two or three hours at a stretch. He would wake in the dark with his heart hammering, certain the truck was still coming. During the day, he avoided driving entirely at first, then began taking only back roads, white-knuckling the steering wheel, scanning every intersection with an alertness that exhausted him. He stopped going to the diner where he had eaten breakfast every Saturday morning for eleven years because it required crossing the same highway where the accident occurred.

What unsettles Gerald most, and what he is most reluctant to admit, is that the accident has stirred things he thought were long settled. He spent decades treating wounded soldiers, holding pressure on wounds, making decisions in seconds. He had always told himself he had processed all of that. Now, unbidden, images from those years surface alongside the memory of the collision — the rearview mirror, a young soldier's face, the smell of burning, the smell of blood — and he cannot always tell which memory belongs to which moment in his life. Everything has become one long emergency he cannot leave.

He lives alone since losing his wife to cancer three years ago, and the solitude that once felt peaceful now feels like exposure. He keeps the television on through the night. He has stopped attending his veterans' group, not because he doesn't want to see the men there, but because he no longer trusts himself to hold it together in front of them. He was their medic once, in one way or another. He does not know how to be anything else in that room.

Gerald presents as a man who is articulate and self-aware, and who has spent a lifetime being the person who does not fall apart. He describes his current state with a kind of bewildered grief, as though he is watching himself from a distance and cannot reconcile what he sees with who he knows himself to be. He says, more than once, that he has seen far worse than a car accident. He says this as though it should mean something, as though the mind is reasonable, as though surviving worse things should have made this one easier to carry.

He is beginning to understand that it does not work that way.
